summary.text:
Ealing's Q4 outturn gives the cleanest reconciliation of the batch. Table 5 splits PWLB three ways — General Fund £480.010m, HRA £148.124m and Broadway Living £86.289m — and the three sum to £714.423m against the £714,422,778 in our own file. To the pound. Every other cell in Table 5 foots too, as do Tables 2, 3, 4 and 6.

Two things stand out. First, paragraph 40 puts the HRA discount on the wrong base: it says the certainty rate allows borrowing at a reduction of 0.20% for the General Fund and 0.40% for the HRA 'on the Standard Rate'. The 0.20% is right, but 0.40% off standard is the Local Infrastructure Rate — the HRA discount of 0.40% runs off the CERTAINTY rate, so 0.60% off standard. That matters here rather than being pedantry, because Table 6 shows the HRA CFR rising £103.975m while HRA debt fell £4.932m: HRA internal borrowing went from £104.022m to £212.929m in a single year, with no new borrowing raised at all. The rate whose basis is misstated is exactly the rate that would close the largest gap in the report. Their Table 4 gets every certainty rate LEVEL right, four for four against our record.

Second, paragraph 50 is unfair to its own authors — it says returns underperformed the SONIA benchmark, where Table 3 shows +0.040% across the year and +0.161% in March 2026, with eight of twelve months positive. We rebuilt both averages and they come out at exactly the printed 4.050% and 4.010%.

Also of record: local authority lending was RESUMED, from nil to £99.000m across twenty councils, now 34.13% of the portfolio. And the book — 112 loans at a weighted 2.9609% — carries about £232.3m of net discount on today's curve, 32.5% of principal, the deepest proportional discount we have computed anywhere. No officer address is published.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Q4 outturn that went to Audit Committee on 22 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first, and yours is the cleanest we have run. Table 5 splits PWLB three ways — General Fund £480.010m, HRA £148.124m and Broadway Living £86.289m — across three separate blocks. Those sum to £714.423m. Our own file holds 112 Ealing loans totalling £714,422,778. To the pound, across a table that no other council in everything we have read splits that way. Every other cell in Table 5 foots as well, as do Tables 2, 4 and 6.

We wrote because of two things that sit either side of the report.

The first is Table 6. Your HRA CFR rose £103.975m in the year, to £382.312m, while HRA debt fell £4.932m to £169.383m. So HRA internal borrowing went from £104.022m to £212.929m — it more than doubled in twelve months, with no new borrowing raised at all. That is the largest single financing gap in the report and it is entirely internal at the moment.

The second is paragraph 40, and it connects directly. It says the certainty rate allows borrowing "at a reduction of 0.20% for General Fund (GF) and 0.40% for Housing Revenue Account (HRA) on the Standard Rate."

The 0.20% is right. The 0.40% is on the wrong base. The margins are standard at gilt plus 100, certainty at gilt plus 80, the Local Infrastructure Rate at gilt plus 60 through the National Wealth Fund, and the HRA rate at gilt plus 40. So 0.40% off the standard rate is the Local Infrastructure Rate; the HRA discount of 0.40% runs off the certainty rate, which makes it 0.60% off standard. Two other councils state it the way round we would expect — Croydon's appendix sets out all four margins in gilt-plus terms, and Enfield's describes the HRA rate as "a further discount of 40 bps" beyond the certainty rate.

We would not raise a twenty basis point definition on its own. We raise it because of the £212.929m above: the rate whose basis is understated in paragraph 40 is precisely the rate at which that gap would eventually be externalised, and twenty basis points on a sum that size is real money in the HRA business plan. It is worth saying that your Table 4 has every certainty rate level right — 5.28, 5.72, 6.29 and 6.08 at 31 March match our own record for that day four for four — so this is a definition in a glossary-style paragraph rather than anything that touched a transaction. You did not draw any PWLB in the year.

The third thing is a correction in your favour. Paragraph 50 says internally managed returns "underperformed the SONIA benchmark on the 31 March 2026". Your Table 3, three pages earlier, shows March 2026 at 3.890% against a benchmark of 3.729% — an outperformance of sixteen basis points — and the full year at plus four basis points, with eight of the twelve months positive and the underperformance confined to April to July 2025. We rebuilt both twelve-month averages from your own monthly figures and they come out at 4.0498% and 4.0101%, exactly the 4.050% and 4.010% you print. The table is right; the sentence sells the year short.

Two shorter notes.

Paragraph 27 records that lending to other local authorities has been resumed, and it went from nil to £99.000m across twenty councils in a year — now 34.13% of the portfolio. You are not alone: Staffordshire's book went from £30m to £152m across twenty-five councils over the same twelve months, and Liverpool raised £118m of two-to-four year money from seventeen. That market deepened sharply in 2025/26, and the pricing in it ranged from about 4.15% to 8.50% over the year end depending on who needed money and when. We publish the distribution because no council can see it from its own trades, at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

And on your paragraph 39, which explains premium and discount correctly: on the DMO's curve this afternoon, 97 of your 112 loans price below par, for about £235.6m of discount against £3.25m of premium on the other fifteen — roughly £232.3m net, which is 32.5% of principal and the deepest proportional discount we have computed for any council. It is the direct consequence of a book costing a weighted 2.9609%. We're not suggesting anything follows: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Yours is priced daily at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, four fit Ealing. PWLB explained covers the rate bases behind paragraph 40, and HRA Liability Benchmark: two-pool goes to the £212.929m. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets goes to the resumed £99m. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator sizes the position above. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management Quarter 4 Outturn 2025/26, Audit Committee, 22 July 2026. Appendices 1 and 2 not held.
